<button id="toc-toggle"
        type="button"
        aria-label="Toggle table of contents"
        aria-expanded="true">
  <span class="menu-icon" aria-hidden="true">&#9776;</span>
  <span class="close-icon" aria-hidden="true">&times;</span>
  <span class="sr-only">Toggle table of contents</span>
</button>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
  const button = document.getElementById("toc-toggle");

  if (!button) return;

  button.addEventListener("click", function () {
    if (window.innerWidth <= 991) {
      document.body.classList.toggle("toc-mobile-open");

      const isOpen =
        document.body.classList.contains("toc-mobile-open");

      button.setAttribute("aria-expanded", isOpen);
    } else {
      document.body.classList.toggle("toc-collapsed");

      const isOpen =
        !document.body.classList.contains("toc-collapsed");

      button.setAttribute("aria-expanded", isOpen);
    }
  });
});
</script>


```{r generate_all_lecture_figures, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  error = FALSE
)

required_packages <- c("ggplot2", "gridExtra", "dplyr", "tidyr")
missing_packages <- required_packages[
  !vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]

if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop(
    "Install the following R packages before knitting: ",
    paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", ")
  )
}

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(gridExtra)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
})

set.seed(123) # Set seed for reproducible figures

# Shared publication-style theme and colour palette.
lecture_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, colour = "#333333"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(8, 10, 8, 10)
  )

palette_main <- c("#4C72B0", "#55A868", "#C44E52", "#8172B2", "#CCB974")

save_plot <- function(filename, plot, width, height) {
  ggsave(
    filename = filename,
    plot = plot,
    width = width,
    height = height,
    units = "in",
    dpi = 300,
    bg = "white"
  )
}

# =============================================================
# 1. Mean vs Median: Skewed Distribution (Viral Load)
# =============================================================
viral_load <- rlnorm(500, meanlog = 4, sdlog = 0.8)
viral_df <- data.frame(load = viral_load)
v_mean <- mean(viral_load)
v_median <- median(viral_load)

p_skewed <- ggplot(viral_df, aes(x = load)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#caced3", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = v_median, colour = palette_main[2], size = 1.2, linetype = "solid") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = v_mean, colour = palette_main[3], size = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = v_median, y = Inf, label = "Median", colour = palette_main[2], vjust = 1.5, hjust = 1.2, fontface="bold") +
  annotate("text", x = v_mean, y = Inf, label = "Mean", colour = palette_main[3], vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.2, fontface="bold") +
  labs(
    title = "Right-Skewed Data: The Mean is Pulled to the Right",
    x = "Viral Load (Copies / mL)",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  lecture_theme

save_plot("fig_ch2_skewed_mean_median.png", p_skewed, width = 6, height = 4)


# =============================================================
# 2. Resistance to Outliers: Small Dotplot Example
# =============================================================
base_data <- c(12, 13, 14, 15, 16)
outlier_data <- c(12, 13, 14, 15, 45)

df_resist <- data.frame(
  Value = c(base_data, outlier_data),
  Group = factor(rep(c("A: Normal Sample", "B: Sample with Outlier"), each = 5))
)

means <- df_resist %>% group_by(Group) %>% summarize(m = mean(Value))
medians <- df_resist %>% group_by(Group) %>% summarize(m = median(Value))

p_resist <- ggplot(df_resist, aes(x = Value, y = Group)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, fill = palette_main[1], colour = "black", shape = 21) +
  geom_point(data = means, aes(x = m, y = Group), shape = 4, size = 5, colour = palette_main[3], stroke = 2) +
  geom_point(data = medians, aes(x = m, y = Group), shape = 3, size = 5, colour = palette_main[2], stroke = 2) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  annotate("text", x = 14, y = 2.3, label = "Median (+) = 14\nMean (x) = 14", size=3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 30, y = 1.3, label = "Median (+) stays at 14\nMean (x) gets pulled to 19.8!", size=3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "The Concept of Resistance to Outliers",
    x = "Measured Value",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  lecture_theme

save_plot("fig_ch2_resistance.png", p_resist, width = 7, height = 3.5)


# =============================================================
# 3. Anatomy of a Boxplot
# =============================================================
box_data <- rnorm(100, mean = 50, sd = 10)
# Force a couple of outliers
box_data <- c(box_data, 15, 85, 92)
box_df <- data.frame(y = box_data, x = factor("A"))

# Calculate 5-number summary
stats <- boxplot.stats(box_df$y)$stats

p_box_anatomy <- ggplot(box_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.4, fill = palette_main[4], alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = 21, outlier.size = 3, outlier.fill = palette_main[3]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = stats[3], label = "Median (Middle 50%)", fontface="bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = stats[4], label = "Q3 (75th Percentile)") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = stats[2], label = "Q1 (25th Percentile)") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = stats[5], label = "Maximum non-outlier") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = stats[1], label = "Minimum non-outlier") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.1, y = 92, label = "Suspected Outliers", colour = palette_main[3], fontface="bold", hjust=0) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.7, xend = 0.7, y = stats[2], yend = stats[4], 
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.1, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = stats[3], label = "IQR\n(Middle 50%\nof data)", angle=90) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "The Anatomy of a Boxplot") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b=10)))

save_plot("fig_ch2_boxplot_anatomy.png", p_box_anatomy, width = 6, height = 5)


# =============================================================
# 4. Side-by-Side Boxplots (CRISPR Efficiency)
# =============================================================
set.seed(42)
crispr_df <- data.frame(
  Method = factor(rep(c("Lipid Nanoparticles", "Viral Vector", "Electroporation"), each = 40),
                  levels = c("Lipid Nanoparticles", "Viral Vector", "Electroporation")),
  Efficiency = c(rnorm(40, 45, 12), rnorm(40, 75, 8), rnorm(40, 30, 15))
)
# Ensure no values outside 0-100
crispr_df$Efficiency <- pmax(0, pmin(100, crispr_df$Efficiency))

p_side_box <- ggplot(crispr_df, aes(x = Method, y = Efficiency, fill = Method)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = 21, outlier.size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = palette_main[1:3]) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparing CRISPR-Cas9 Delivery Methods",
    x = "Delivery Vector Type",
    y = "Target Cell Editing Efficiency (%)"
  ) +
  lecture_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

save_plot("fig_ch2_side_by_side_boxplots.png", p_side_box, width = 7, height = 4)


# =============================================================
# 5. Understanding Standard Deviation
# =============================================================
x_val <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 1000)
y_val <- dnorm(x_val)
sd_df <- data.frame(x = x_val, y = y_val)

p_sd <- ggplot(sd_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_area(data = subset(sd_df, x >= -1 & x <= 1), fill = palette_main[1], alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0.15, xend = 1, yend = 0.15), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")), size=0.8, colour="black") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.17, label = "+1 Standard Deviation (s)", fontface="bold") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2), labels = c( "-2s", "-1s", "Mean (x̄)", "+1s", "+2s")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  labs(
    title = "Standard Deviation: The 'Average' Distance from the Mean",
    x = "Measured Values",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  lecture_theme

save_plot("fig_ch2_standard_deviation.png", p_sd, width = 6, height = 3.5)
```

# Chapter 2: Describing Distributions with Numbers {.chapter-root .unlisted}

## Describing Distributions with Numbers

### The Limits of Human Perception

In Chapter 1, we learned that the first rule of modern data analysis is to **always plot your data**. Visualizations like histograms and dotplots allow our eyes to quickly spot shapes, trends, bimodal clusters, and data entry errors.

However, human eyes are subjective. If you ask two different scientists to look at a slightly skewed histogram and point to the "center," they will likely point to two different spots. If we want to write a reproducible research paper or train a machine-learning model, we cannot rely on pointing.

We need to translate our visual descriptions—**Shape, Outliers, Center, and Spread (SOCS)**—into objective, mathematical summaries.

---

<!-- ### Chapter Learning Objectives -->

<!-- 4. Construct the **five-number summary** and use it to build and interpret **boxplots**. -->
<!-- 5. Use the $1.5 \times IQR$ rule to objectively flag suspected outliers. -->
<!-- 6. Calculate and interpret the **standard deviation** ($s$) as a measure of spread. -->
<!-- 7. Choose the appropriate set of numerical summaries based on the shape of the data. -->

---

## Measuring Center: Mean and Median

When a biologist asks, *"What is the typical length of a pine needle?"* or *"What is the normal number of flood events on the coast?"*, they are asking for a measure of **center**. Statistics gives us two primary ways to define "typical," and they behave very differently depending on the shape of the data.

### The Mean ($\bar{x}$)

The most commonly reported measure of center is the ordinary arithmetic average, or **mean**. To find the mean of a set of observations, you add their values together and divide by the number of observations ($n$).

If the $n$ observations are $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$, their sample mean is:

$$ \bar{x} = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n}{n} $$

In statistics, we use the uppercase Greek letter sigma ($\sum$) as the mathematical symbol for summation (which just means "add them all up"). Therefore, the compact formula for the mean is: 

$$ \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum x_i $$

> **Notation Note:** We use $\bar{x}$ (pronounced "x-bar") to represent the mean of a *sample* of data. Later in the course, we will use the Greek letter $\mu$ (mu) to represent the theoretical mean of an entire *population*.

#### Example 2.3: Mean of Pine Needle Lengths

Let's find the mean needle length for a sample of $15$ Aleppo pine needles. First, we can organize our $n = 15$ observations ($x_i$) into a table:

| Observation ($i$) | Length $x_i$ (cm) | | Observation ($i$) | Length $x_i$ (cm) | | Observation ($i$) | Length $x_i$ (cm) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1** | 7.2 | | **6** | 9.0 | | **11** | 10.2 |
| **2** | 7.6 | | **7** | 9.0 | | **12** | 10.9 |
| **3** | 8.5 | | **8** | 9.3 | | **13** | 11.3 |
| **4** | 8.5 | | **9** | 9.4 | | **14** | 12.1 |
| **5** | 8.7 | | **10** | 9.4 | | **15** | 12.8 |

To calculate the mean, we first use the summation notation ($\sum$) to add up all $15$ individual lengths:

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{15} x_i = 143.9 \text{ cm} $$

Next, we divide that total sum by the number of observations ($n = 15$):

$$ \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{15} x_i = \frac{143.9}{15} \approx 9.59 \text{ cm} $$

*In practice, you will type this data into a calculator or statistical software, which will label the output as "Mean" or "$\bar{x}$". However, paying attention to the formula reminds us of a critical fact: **the mean uses the actual numerical value of every single observation in the dataset.***

**Calculating the Mean in R:**
```{r, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
# Create a vector of the 15 pine needle lengths
aleppo_needles <- c(7.2, 7.6, 8.5, 8.5, 8.7, 9.0, 9.0, 9.3, 9.4, 9.4, 10.2, 10.9, 11.3, 12.1, 12.8)
                    
# Calculate the mean
mean(aleppo_needles)                    
```

### The Median ($M$)

The **median** is the exact geometric midpoint of a distribution. It is the 50th percentile—the number such that exactly half (50%) of the observations are smaller and the other half are larger.

To find the median by hand:

1. **Sort** all observations in order of size, from smallest to largest.
2. Use the location rule: the median is always located at position **$\frac{n+1}{2}$** in the ordered list.
3. If $n$ is **odd**, this location lands on a single center number. If $n$ is **even**, this location lands between two numbers, and you must take their exact average.

> **Software Note:** Different statistical programs label the median slightly differently. You will typically see it called **"Median"** or **"Med"**, but SPSS labels it **"Percentile 50"** and JMP calls it a **"Quantile."** They all mean the exact same center point!

#### Example: Finding the Median

**Example 2.1: Aleppo Pine Needles (Odd $n$)**  
What is the median length for our $15$ Aleppo pine needles?

| Step | Action | Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1.** | Sort the data | 7.2, 7.6, 8.5, 8.5, 8.7, 9.0, 9.0, **9.3**, 9.4, 9.4, 10.2, 10.9, 11.3, 12.1, 12.8 |
| **2.** | Locate the median | $\frac{n+1}{2} = \frac{15+1}{2} = 8$ |
| **3.** | Find the middle | The 8th observation in the sorted list is 9.3 cm. |
| | **Result** | **Median ($M$) = 9.3 cm** |

```{r, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
# Using our aleppo_needles vector from earlier
median(aleppo_needles)
```

**Example 2.2: Torrey Pine Needles (Even $n$)**  
Now we have the lengths of $18$ needles from a noticeably different species, the Torrey pine. 

| Step | Action | Result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1.** | Sort the data | 21.2, 21.6, 21.7, 23.1, 23.7, 24.2, 24.2, 25.5, **26.6, 26.8**, 28.9, 29.0, 29.7, 29.7, 30.2, 32.5, 33.7, 33.7 |
| **2.** | Locate the median | $\frac{n+1}{2} = \frac{18+1}{2} = 9.5$ |
| **3.** | Find the middle | The location 9.5 means halfway between the 9th and 10th observations: $\frac{26.6 + 26.8}{2}$ |
| | **Result** | **Median ($M$) = 26.7 cm** |

Calculating the Median in R (Even $n$):
```{r, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
# Create a vector of the 18 Torrey pine needle lengths
torrey_needles <- c(21.2, 21.6, 21.7, 23.1, 23.7, 24.2, 24.2, 25.5, 26.6, 
                    26.8, 28.9, 29.0, 29.7, 29.7, 30.2, 32.5, 33.7, 33.7)

# Calculate the median
median(torrey_needles)
```


---


## Comparing the Mean and the Median: Resistance

If both the mean and the median measure the "center," why do we need both? We need them because they react differently to extreme biology.

Let's look at the recovery times of our first 5 patients again. For roughly symmetric data, the mean and median are very close together:

*   **Sorted Data:** 4, 6, 7, 8, 9
*   **Median:** 7 days
*   **Mean:** $\frac{4+6+7+8+9}{5} = 6.8$ days

But what happens if our 5th patient is a "long-hauler" who takes **45 days** to recover instead of 9?

Our new dataset is: 4, 6, 7, 8, 45.

<img src="fig_ch2_resistance.png" alt="Dotplot showing a normal sample vs a sample with an outlier, illustrating how the mean is pulled while the median stays fixed." />

| Statistic | Normal Sample (4, 6, 7, 8, 9) | Outlier Sample (4, 6, 7, 8, **45**) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Median ($M$)** | 7 days | **7 days** (It didn't change at all!) |
| **Mean ($\bar{x}$)** | 6.8 days | **14 days** (Drastically pulled to the right) |

### The Concept of Resistance

A statistical measure is called **resistant** (or robust) if it is not strongly influenced by a few extreme observations (outliers).

*   **The median is resistant:** Because it only cares about the physical *order* of the numbers, you can change the largest number to a million, and the median won't budge.
*   **The mean is non-resistant:** Because the mean mathematically incorporates the exact value of every single observation, a single massive outlier will drag the mean toward it.

### Shape Determines the Center

Because of this concept of resistance, the visual shape of your histogram immediately tells you how the mean and median will relate to each other mathematically.

<img src="fig_ch2_skewed_mean_median.png" alt="Histogram of right-skewed viral load data showing the mean pulled to the right of the median." />

| Distribution Shape | Mathematical Relationship | Biological Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Symmetric** | Mean $\approx$ Median | Adult penguin body masses. Both sit in the center of the symmetric peak. |
| **Skewed Right** | Mean $>$ Median | Viral loads. Extreme high values in the long right tail act like heavy weights, pulling the mean to the right. |
| **Skewed Left** | Mean $<$ Median | Age at retirement. Extreme low values drag the mean to the left. |

> **First-Year Rule of Thumb:**  
> The mean is always drawn toward the long tail of a skewed distribution. If the tail points to the right, the mean gets pulled to the right of the median!

---

## Measuring Spread: Quartiles and Boxplots

Saying that the median penguin weighs **4.5 kg** tells us the center, but it doesn't tell us how widely penguin weights vary. Are most penguins exactly **4.5 kg**, or do they range wildly from **2 kg** to **8 kg**? A measure of center must always be accompanied by a measure of **spread** (variability).

### The Quartiles ($Q_1$ and $Q_3$)

Just as the median divides the data exactly in half, the quartiles divide the data into exactly four equal quarters.

*   **Quartile 1 ($Q_1$):** The median of the lower half of the data. Exactly **25%** of the data falls below $Q_1$.
*   **Quartile 3 ($Q_3$):** The median of the upper half of the data. Exactly **75%** of the data falls below $Q_3$ (and **25%** is above it).

**To calculate the quartiles by hand:**
1.  Sort the data and find the overall Median ($M$).
2.  Locate the lower half of the data. *(Note: If $n$ is odd, do not include the overall median in this lower half).* The median of this lower half is $Q_1$.
3.  Locate the upper half of the data. The median of this upper half is $Q_3$.

> **Data Entry Tip:**  
> Be careful when several observations take the exact same numerical value. Include all the duplicate observations in your list and apply the rules just as if they all had distinct values!

---

#### Example 2.5: Finding the Quartiles (Odd $n$)

Let's find the quartiles for our sample of $15$ Aleppo pine needles. Here are the data, arranged in increasing order:

| | Lower Half | Median | Upper Half |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Values** | 7.2, 7.6, 8.5, **8.5**, 8.7, 9.0, 9.0 | **9.3** | 9.4, 9.4, 10.2, **10.9**, 11.3, 12.1, 12.8 |

We have an odd number of observations ($n=15$), so the overall median is the middle one: **$M = 9.3$ cm**.

*   **Finding $Q_1$:** The first quartile is the median of the 7 observations to the left of $9.3$. With $n=7$, the middle is the 4th observation.
    *   **$Q_1 = 8.5$ cm**
*   **Finding $Q_3$:** The third quartile is the median of the 7 observations to the right of $9.3$.
    *   **$Q_3 = 10.9$ cm**

Notice that the quartiles are highly **resistant to outliers**. For example, $Q_3$ would still be $10.9$ cm even if the largest needle length was a massive $50$ cm rather than $12.8$ cm!

Finding Quartiles and the Five-Number Summary in R:
```{r, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
# The summary() function gives the min, Q1, median, mean, Q3, and max all at once.

# Aleppo pines (Odd n)
summary(aleppo_needles)
```

---

#### Example 2.6: Finding the Quartiles (Even $n$)

Now let's look at the lengths of the $18$ Torrey pine needles, arranged in increasing order:

| | Lower Half | | Upper Half |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Values** | 21.2, 21.6, 21.7, 23.1, **23.7**, 24.2, 24.2, 25.5, 26.6 | *(Median = 26.7)* | 26.8, 28.9, 29.0, 29.7, **29.7**, 30.2, 32.5, 33.7, 33.7 |

We have an even number of observations ($n=18$). As we found earlier, the overall median lies exactly midway between the 9th and 10th values (26.6 and 26.8), so **$M = 26.7$ cm**.

*   **Finding $Q_1$:** The first quartile is the median of the first 9 observations (since these are all strictly to the left of our median location). The middle of 9 items is the 5th value.
    *   **$Q_1 = 23.7$ cm**
*   **Finding $Q_3$:** The third quartile is the median of the upper 9 observations. 
    *   **$Q_3 = 29.7$ cm**

```{r, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
# Torrey pines (Even n)
summary(torrey_needles)
```

> **Why does R give a slightly different answer?**  
> If you type the 15 Aleppo pine needle lengths into different programs, you might notice small differences. A graphing calculator might say $Q_1 = 8.5$, but R might say $Q_1 = 8.6$. 
> 
> *How can this be?* There are actually several different mathematical rules (interpolation algorithms) for finding quartiles when the splits aren't perfectly even. Our hand-calculation rule is the simplest way to perform the computations manually. The computer's rules give slightly different, but always very close, answers. When analyzing real data in the lab, **always trust the output your software package gives you!**

---

### The Interquartile Range (IQR)

The distance between the first and third quartiles is called the **Interquartile Range**. 

$$IQR = Q_3 - Q_1$$

The IQR is the exact span of the **middle 50%** of your data. Because the IQR completely ignores the bottom 25% and top 25% of the data, it is a highly **resistant** measure of spread. A giant outlier in the tail will not affect the width of the middle 50%.

Calculating IQR in R:
```{r, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
IQR(aleppo_needles)

IQR(torrey_needles)
```

---

### The Five-Number Summary

By combining our measures of center, our measures of spread, and the absolute extremes of our data, we get a highly efficient snapshot of the entire distribution called the **five-number summary**:

$$ \text{Minimum} \quad Q_1 \quad \text{Median} \quad Q_3 \quad \text{Maximum} $$

These five numbers offer a reasonably complete mathematical description of a dataset's center and spread.

---

### Boxplots: Visualizing the Five-Number Summary

A **boxplot** is a graph built directly from the five-number summary. While histograms are great for showing the shape of a single dataset, boxplots are the gold standard in the life sciences for comparing multiple groups side-by-side.

<img src="fig_ch2_boxplot_anatomy.png" alt="Annotated diagram of a boxplot showing quartiles, median, and outliers." />

#### How to Read a Boxplot

*   The central **box** spans from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$. The width of this box is the exact **IQR** (the middle **50%** of the data).
*   The thick line inside the box is the **Median**.
*   Lines (called **whiskers**) extend outward from the box to the smallest and largest observations *that are not considered outliers*.
*   Individual dots floating beyond the whiskers are suspected **outliers**.

#### Side-by-Side Comparisons

Why are boxplots so popular in modern biology? Because they allow us to compare dozens of experimental groups cleanly in a single graphic. 

Suppose researchers are testing three different methods for delivering CRISPR-Cas9 genome editors into a patient's cells: *Lipid Nanoparticles*, *Viral Vectors*, and *Electroporation*.

<img src="fig_ch2_side_by_side_boxplots.png" alt="Side-by-side boxplots showing CRISPR editing efficiency across three delivery methods." />

A quick glance at this boxplot reveals:

*   **Center:** Viral vectors yield the highest median editing efficiency.
*   **Spread:** Electroporation is highly unstable (the IQR box is very tall, meaning highly variable results).
*   **Outliers:** Lipid nanoparticles are generally consistent, but had a few cells that successfully edited at an unexpectedly high rate (the two outlier dots).

---

## Identifying Outliers: The $1.5 \times IQR$ Rule

In Chapter 1, we said an outlier is an observation that falls "well outside" the overall pattern. But "well outside" is a subjective judgment. How does R or Python automatically know which dots to plot outside the whiskers of a boxplot?

Statisticians use an objective mathematical formula called the **$1.5 \times IQR$ Rule** to flag suspected outliers.

#### The Outlier Formula
An observation is flagged as a suspected outlier if it falls more than $1.5 \times IQR$ above the third quartile or below the first quartile.

| Boundary | Formula |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Upper Fence** | $Q_3 + (1.5 \times IQR)$ |
| **Lower Fence** | $Q_1 - (1.5 \times IQR)$ |

Any data point larger than the Upper Fence or smaller than the Lower Fence is plotted as an individual dot.

```{r outlier_rule, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
# Sample vector of needle lengths with an added extreme value (15.8)
data <- c(7.2, 7.6, 8.5, 8.5, 8.7, 9.0, 9.0, 9.3, 9.4, 9.4, 10.2, 10.9, 11.3, 12.1, 15.8)

# 1. Calculate Q1, Q3, and IQR
q1 <- quantile(data, 0.25)
q3 <- quantile(data, 0.75)
iqr_val <- IQR(data)

# 2. Calculate Upper and Lower Fences
lower_fence <- q1 - (1.5 * iqr_val)
upper_fence <- q3 + (1.5 * iqr_val)

# Display the boundary fences
c(Lower_Fence = lower_fence, Upper_Fence = upper_fence)

# 3. Identify values outside the fences
outliers <- data[data < lower_fence | data > upper_fence]
outliers
```

> **Exam Warning:**  
> This mathematical rule tells you *that* a data point is mathematically unusual, but it does **NOT** give you permission to delete it! You must investigate the biology or lab methodology before removing any outlier.

---

## Measuring Spread: The Standard Deviation ($s$)

If we use the Median to measure center, we use the IQR to measure spread. 
But if we use the Mean ($\bar{x}$) to measure center, we need a different measure of spread: the **Standard Deviation** ($s$).

The standard deviation measures spread by looking at how far each individual observation falls from the mean. Conceptually, you can think of standard deviation as the **"average distance"** of all the data points from the center.

<img src="fig_ch2_standard_deviation.png" alt="Density curve illustrating one standard deviation from the mean." />

### The Math Behind Standard Deviation

To calculate how far the data is spread out, we first find the distance (deviation) of each point from the mean: $(x_i - \bar{x})$. 

However, if we just added these distances up, the negative distances (points below the mean) would exactly cancel out the positive distances (points above the mean), resulting in a sum of zero. 

To fix this, we **square** the distances to make them all positive, average them, and then take the **square root** to get back to our original biological units.

*   The **Variance** ($s^2$) is the average of the squared distances:
    $$ s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 $$

*   The **Standard Deviation** ($s$) is the square root of the variance:
    $$ s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2} $$

> **Why $(n-1)$ instead of $n$?**  
> Notice that we divide by $(n-1)$ instead of $n$. This is called **degrees of freedom**. Because we already used our sample data to estimate the mean ($\bar{x}$), we "spent" one piece of independent information. Dividing by $(n-1)$ corrects a mathematical bias, ensuring our sample standard deviation perfectly estimates the true population spread.

---

### Example 2.7: Calculating the Standard Deviation (Metabolic Rates)

A person’s metabolic rate is the rate at which the body consumes energy. Here are the metabolic rates of $7$ men who took part in a dieting study. The units are kilocalories (Cal) for a 24-hour period.

**Raw Data ($n=7$):** 1792, 1666, 1362, 1614, 1460, 1867, 1439

**Step 1: Find the Mean ($\bar{x}$)**
$$ \bar{x} = \frac{1792 + 1666 + 1362 + 1614 + 1460 + 1867 + 1439}{7} = \frac{11{,}200}{7} = 1600 \text{ Cal} $$

**Step 2: Find the Deviations and Square Them**
Now we subtract the mean ($1600$) from every observation, and square the result. 

| Observation ($x_i$) | Deviation from Mean ($x_i - \bar{x}$) | Squared Deviation $(x_i - \bar{x})^2$ |
| :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **1792** | $1792 - 1600 = 192$ | $192^2 = 36{,}864$ |
| **1666** | $1666 - 1600 = 66$ | $66^2 = 4{,}356$ |
| **1362** | $1362 - 1600 = -238$ | $(-238)^2 = 56{,}644$ |
| **1614** | $1614 - 1600 = 14$ | $14^2 = 196$ |
| **1460** | $1460 - 1600 = -140$ | $(-140)^2 = 19{,}600$ |
| **1867** | $1867 - 1600 = 267$ | $267^2 = 71{,}289$ |
| **1439** | $1439 - 1600 = -161$ | $(-161)^2 = 25{,}921$ |
| | **Sum of Deviations = 0** | **Sum of Squares = 214,870** |

*Notice that the sum of the un-squared deviations is exactly zero. This will always happen, which is why we must square them!*

**Step 3: Calculate Variance ($s^2$)**
Divide the sum of squared deviations by $n - 1$ (which is $7 - 1 = 6$):
$$ s^2 = \frac{214{,}870}{6} = 35{,}811.67 \text{ Cal}^2 $$

**Step 4: Calculate Standard Deviation ($s$)**
Take the square root of the variance to return to the original biological units:
$$ s = \sqrt{35{,}811.67} = 189.24 \text{ Cal} $$

**Conclusion:** The men burn an average of **1600 Cal** per day, and their individual metabolic rates typically vary from that mean by about **189.24 Cal**.

```{r, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE}
# Create a vector of the 7 metabolic rates
metabolic_rates <- c(1792, 1666, 1362, 1614, 1460, 1867, 1439)

# Calculate the sample variance (s^2)
var(metabolic_rates)
#> [1] 35811.67

# Calculate the sample standard deviation (s)
sd(metabolic_rates)
#> [1] 189.2397
```
---

### Properties of the Standard Deviation

*   **$s$ measures spread around the mean.** It should only be used when the mean is chosen as the measure of center.
*   **$s = 0$ only when there is zero spread.** This means all observations have the exact same value. Otherwise, $s$ is always greater than zero.
*   **$s$ has the same units of measurement as the original observations.** If you measure metabolic rate in Calories, the standard deviation is in Calories. (The variance would be in $\text{Calories}^2$, which is biologically unhelpful to talk about).
*   **$s$ is non-resistant!** Because the formula uses the mean and squares the distances, a single extreme outlier will inflate the standard deviation drastically.

---

## Choosing the Right Summary

You now have two complete sets of tools to summarize a quantitative distribution:
1.  **The Mean and Standard Deviation** ($\bar{x}$ and $s$).
2.  **The Five-Number Summary** ($\text{Minimum}$, $Q_1$, $M$, $Q_3$, $\text{Maximum}$).

How do you know which one to report in your research paper? It depends entirely on the **Shape** and **Outliers** of your distribution!

| When to Use | Mean & Standard Deviation | Median & IQR (Five-Number) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Shape** | Reasonably Symmetric | Skewed (Left or Right) |
| **Outliers** | No extreme outliers | Contains suspected outliers |
| **Why?** | These are **non-resistant**. They mathematically incorporate every value, making them powerful for normal biology, but easily ruined by extreme values. | These are **resistant**. They ignore the extreme tails of the data, providing a stable snapshot of "typical" biology even when outliers are present. |

> **Real-World Example:**  
> If you are measuring the wingspans of 100 monarch butterflies, the data will likely be symmetric and bell-shaped. You should report the **Mean and Standard Deviation**.  
>  
> If you are measuring the circulating viral load in 100 COVID-19 patients, the data will be severely right-skewed (most people have moderate viral loads, but a few "super-spreaders" will have loads 10,000x higher). You should report the **Median and IQR**.

---

## Summary: Descriptive Statistics Checklist

When asked to summarize a quantitative dataset, always follow this workflow:

*   **Plot the data first:** Use a histogram or dotplot to check for shape and outliers.
*   **Choose your tools:**
    *   If symmetric $\rightarrow$ use **Mean** ($\bar{x}$) and **Standard Deviation** ($s$).
    *   If skewed or has outliers $\rightarrow$ use **Median** ($M$) and **IQR**.
*   **Calculate resistance:** Remember that the mean is pulled toward the long tail of a skewed distribution, while the median stands its ground.
*   **Visualize comparisons:** Use side-by-side **boxplots** to compare the five-number summaries of different experimental groups.
*   **Check for outliers mathematically:** Use the **$1.5 \times IQR$ rule** to flag unusual points, but investigate them scientifically before deciding to exclude them.
